title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
description: Make AI reason step by step — the technique that produces dramatically better results on complex problems.

data.text: Chain-of-thought prompting is one of the most well-researched improvements in prompt engineering. It works by asking the AI to show its reasoning before giving an answer — and this dramatically reduces errors on complex tasks. The simple phrase "think step by step" can double accuracy on reasoning problems.
Why it works

When an LLM generates a reasoning chain before its final answer, each step conditions the next step. The model is essentially writing its working notes, and those notes guide it toward a more logical conclusion. Without this, it jumps straight to an answer — often missing intermediate reasoning that would have corrected an error.

data.caption: Without chain-of-thought, the AI jumps to an answer. With it, reasoning becomes a visible chain where each step grounds the next

data.text: How to trigger chain-of-thought

rows: Most analytical tasks — easiest to use
"First identify the key factors. Then rank them. Then recommend."
"Walk me through your reasoning, then give your conclusion."
High-stakes answers where you want to check the logic
"What is the strongest argument AGAINST this conclusion?"
"Argue for the best option from multiple perspectives, then give your verdict."

data.text: Before and after: real examples

data.title: Job offer — without chain-of-thought
data.content:
"Should I accept this job offer?"

→ Gets a generic pros/cons list that could apply to anyone. Not personalized, not contextual, probably not useful.

data.title: Job offer — with chain-of-thought
data.content:
"I have a job offer 20% higher salary, fully remote, at an early-stage startup (Series A). My current role is stable, mid-size company, 5-min commute. I value career growth and financial security equally.

Think through this step by step:
1. Analyze the financial impact (salary, equity, benefits)
2. Assess career growth trajectory at each company
3. Evaluate lifestyle factors (remote vs commute, company culture signals)
4. Weigh the risks specific to an early-stage startup
5. Give a recommendation with your reasoning."

→ Returns a genuinely personalized analysis that actually helps you decide.

data.title: Business problem — with chain-of-thought
data.content: "My SaaS product's monthly churn rate increased from 3% to 7% in the last 60 days. I haven't changed pricing. Think step by step through the most likely causes and rank them by probability. Then describe the first diagnostic action I should take for each."

data.text: When chain-of-thought helps most

rows: Forces consideration of all relevant factors before concluding
Chains through steps prevents jumping to wrong first hypothesis
Some help — but for real math use the code interpreter
Unnecessary overhead when the answer is direct
Less relevant — free generation is usually better here

data.text: For the most critical decisions, ask the AI to first argue FOR the option, then argue AGAINST it, then give a final weighing. This two-sided analysis surfaces blind spots you might not have considered.

data.title: Key points
points: Adding "think step by step" is the simplest and most powerful prompt upgrade
Chain-of-thought improves accuracy by making reasoning process visible and sequential
Most valuable for decisions, analysis, root cause, and planning tasks
Combine with role-play for even better results: "As a CFO, think step by step through..."

data.text: Beginner's guide: simple templates

Start small: use short, explicit prompts that ask for steps. Below are beginner-friendly templates you can copy and adapt. Each template is intentionally explicit about the structure you want the model to produce.

rows: "Think step by step and explain your reasoning before the final answer."
Quick analytical questions where you want the model's chain
"List the steps you would take, explain each step, then give the final recommendation."
"As an experienced product manager, think step by step about how to prioritize these features."
"Example 1: [short Q + step-by-step answer]. Example 2: [short Q + step-by-step answer]. Now solve: [new Q]. Think step by step."
When you can provide examples to guide the model's reasoning style

data.text: Advanced techniques
Once you're comfortable with basic CoT, try these advanced patterns: self-consistency, tree-of-thought, scratchpad, and few-shot CoT. They improve robustness and reduce brittle single-path reasoning.

data.caption: Self-consistency: sample multiple reasoning chains and aggregate
data.definition:
graph TD
  Q["Question"] --> G1["Generate chain 1"]
  Q --> G2["Generate chain 2"]
  Q --> G3["Generate chain 3"]
  G1 --> A1["Answer 1"]
  G2 --> A2["Answer 2"]
  G3 --> A3["Answer 3"]
  A1 --> V["Vote / aggregate"]
  A2 --> V
  A3 --> V
  V --> Final["Final answer (most consistent)"]

  style Q fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style Final fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: Self-consistency works by sampling multiple chains of thought (e.g., with temperature > 0) and then aggregating the final answers (majority vote or confidence-weighted). This reduces reliance on a single reasoning path and often improves accuracy on hard problems.
Tree-of-Thoughts and multi-branch planning

Tree-of-thoughts expands CoT by exploring multiple reasoning branches in parallel, pruning low-quality branches, and synthesizing the best path. Use it for combinatorial problems, planning, and tasks where exploring alternatives is essential.

data.caption: Tree-of-Thoughts: expand, evaluate, prune, synthesize
data.definition:
graph TD
  Q["Problem"] --> B1["Branch A: substep 1"]
  Q --> B2["Branch B: substep 1"]
  B1 --> B1a["Branch A.1: substep 2"]
  B1 --> B1b["Branch A.2: substep 2"]
  B2 --> B2a["Branch B.1: substep 2"]
  B2 --> B2b["Branch B.2: substep 2"]
  B1a --> E1["Evaluate & prune"]
  B2a --> E2["Evaluate & prune"]
  E1 --> S["Synthesize best path"]
  E2 --> S

  style Q fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style S fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: Prompt templates: beginner to advanced

rows: "Think step by step and explain each step."
Short, low-friction; works for many tasks
"Provide a numbered chain of reasoning, then a concise conclusion with confidence level (low/medium/high)."
Adds a confidence signal to help triage answers
"Generate three independent chains of thought (label them A, B, C). For each chain, give the final answer. Then aggregate the answers and explain why you chose the aggregate."
"Use a tree-of-thought approach: propose candidate subgoals, expand each subgoal into reasoning branches, prune low-probability branches, then synthesize a final solution."
Requires careful prompt engineering and often higher compute

data.text: How to evaluate chain-of-thought outputs

rows: Does the chain cover all relevant factors?
Ensures no major assumption is omitted
Are factual claims supported or verifiable?
Is the chain as short as possible while remaining correct?
Reduces noise and improves human review speed
Do repeated runs produce similar conclusions?
Does the model's stated confidence match empirical accuracy?
Helps triage which outputs need verification

data.text: Chain-of-thought makes reasoning visible but does not guarantee truth. Always verify factual claims and be cautious with high-stakes decisions. CoT can increase the surface area for hallucinations if the model invents unsupported intermediate facts.
Pitfalls and limitations

Common issues include verbose or irrelevant chains, overconfidence in incorrect steps, and exposure of private data when prompts include sensitive context. CoT is less useful for short factual lookups and can be computationally more expensive when sampling multiple chains. It can also produce plausible-sounding but incorrect intermediate steps — always verify.
Practical workflows and integrations

Integrate CoT into your product or workflow by: (1) using short CoT prompts for user-facing explanations, (2) running self-consistency in the background for critical answers, and (3) surfacing the chain to users when transparency is required (e.g., legal, medical, or financial contexts) while adding a verification step.

data.caption: Example integration: user query → CoT generation → verification → final answer
data.definition:
graph TD
  U["User query"] --> C["Generate chain-of-thought"]
  C --> V["Automated verification checks"]
  V --> H["Human review (if flagged)"]
  H --> F["Final answer delivered to user"]
  V --> F

  style U fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style F fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: Prompt collection: copy-and-paste examples
Below are ready-to-use prompts for different levels. Use them as starting points and adapt to your domain and tone.

rows: "Please think step by step and explain your reasoning before giving the final answer."
"Example: Q1... A1 (with steps). Example: Q2... A2 (with steps). Now Q3: [your question]. Provide step-by-step reasoning then answer."
When you can provide short examples to set style
"Generate three independent chains of reasoning (A, B, C) and provide the final answer for each. Then aggregate the answers and explain the aggregation."
High-accuracy tasks where sampling is affordable
"List subgoals, expand each subgoal into possible reasoning branches, prune unlikely branches, then synthesize a final solution with steps."

data.text: Advanced example: math + self-consistency

data.title: Multi-path arithmetic reasoning
data.content: "Compute 17 * 24. Generate two independent chains of reasoning (A and B). Show steps for each chain, compute the product, then confirm both results match and give the final answer."

data.text: This forces the model to show two independent calculations; if they disagree, the system can flag the answer for re-evaluation or run a deterministic calculator to verify.
Additional resources and references
Below are curated readings, tutorials, and tools to deepen your understanding from introductory to research-level material.

Practical examples and templates for applied prompt engineering
Hands-on demonstrations including step-by-step reasoning prompts
Practical prompting strategies and examples for production use

data.text: When accuracy matters, combine CoT with external tools (calculators, databases, or verification scripts) rather than relying solely on the model's internal arithmetic or facts.
Conclusion and next steps

Chain-of-thought prompting is a practical, high-impact technique for improving reasoning in LLMs. Start with simple prompts, measure improvements, and progressively adopt advanced patterns like self-consistency and tree-of-thought for the hardest tasks. Always pair CoT with verification for high-stakes use.
